name: The Problem of Universals
statement: When many things share a feature, is there one repeatable entity they share, or only the particulars?
meaning: The problem of universals is one of the oldest and most central problems in metaphysics, concerning the ontological status of the properties and relations that many distinct particular things can share or have in common. When two apples are both red, or two figures both triangular, they seem to share an attribute; the problem asks whether there really exists a single, repeatable entity, a universal such as redness or triangularity, that is wholly present in each of the many particulars, the one-over-many problem going back to Plato, or whether only particular things exist and talk of universals is a mere manner of speaking. A universal is standardly characterized as something that can be instantiated or exemplified by many distinct particulars at once, and so is repeatable, in contrast to a particular, a concrete individual that is not repeatable. The main positions are three. Realism about universals holds that universals really exist, and comes in a Platonic form, on which universals exist independently of and prior to their instances, even uninstantiated, in a separate abstract realm, and an Aristotelian or immanent form, on which universals exist only in the particulars that instantiate them, associated with D. M. Armstrong. Nominalism denies universals, holding that only particulars exist. Trope theory holds that there are properties but they are themselves particulars, tropes, with resemblance among them doing the work. The debate connects to abstract objects, predication, resemblance, and natural kinds.
mechanism: The problem is generated by the phenomenon of shared nature, the fact that numerically distinct things can be alike, can have the same character. Plato's one-over-many argument runs that when many particulars are all F, there must be some one thing, the Form or universal F-ness, in virtue of which they are all F and to which the single predicate F answers. Realists accept this and posit universals as the shared entities that ground objective resemblance and predication, but they divide over where universals reside. Platonic, ante rem realism places universals in a transcendent realm, existing independently of their instances and even if never instantiated, so that redness would exist whether or not anything red did. Aristotelian, in rebus realism places universals in the particulars themselves, wholly present in each red thing and nowhere else, denying uninstantiated universals; on Armstrong's scientific version, which universals there are is a matter for total science to discover. Nominalists reject universals altogether and must explain shared nature using only particulars, through predicate nominalism, on which things are F merely because the predicate F applies to them, resemblance nominalism, on which things are F in virtue of resembling paradigm F things, class nominalism, on which a property is the class of things that have it, or austere, sometimes ostrich, nominalism associated with Quine, which denies that the one-over-many needs any ontological explanation at all. Trope theory takes a middle path: this apple's redness is a particular trope distinct from that apple's redness, and things count as red in virtue of their tropes resembling one another. Classic arguments in the debate include Plato's one over many and the regress worries, notably the Third Man regress against Plato.

examples.text: Many red things all being red suggests, for the realist, one repeatable universal, redness, present in each.
Platonic realism puts universals in a separate realm even uninstantiated; Aristotelian realism puts them only in their instances.
Nominalists explain shared nature by predicates, resemblance, or classes of particulars, without positing universals.

variants.name: Realism, nominalism, trope theory
variants.text: Universals exist; only particulars exist; or properties exist but as particular tropes bound by resemblance.

variants.name: Platonic versus immanent realism
variants.text: Universals in a transcendent realm, prior to instances, versus universals wholly present only in their instances.

whyItMatters: The problem of universals is a perennial and foundational question in metaphysics, debated for over two thousand years from Plato and Aristotle through the great medieval controversy to contemporary analytic philosophy. It matters because it concerns the basic inventory of reality: whether, in addition to the concrete particular things we encounter, there also exist repeatable natures, universals, that many things can share, or whether the world contains only particulars. How one answers reverberates through the rest of metaphysics and beyond, shaping accounts of predication and language, of objective resemblance and similarity, of natural kinds and the laws of nature, and of abstract objects such as numbers. Realism promises a straightforward explanation of why distinct things can be genuinely alike, at the cost of an expanded ontology; nominalism honors ontological economy and Ockham's razor, at the cost of having to explain shared nature by other means; trope theory seeks the advantages of both. The debate has also generated famous arguments and regresses, including the one over many and the Third Man. As the question of whether repeatable universals exist or only particulars do, the problem of universals sits at the very heart of metaphysics.

working.text: observe that distinct particulars can be genuinely alike, sharing a character to which a common predicate answers.
consider whether a single repeatable universal explains the likeness, or whether particulars alone suffice.
adopt realism, nominalism, or trope theory, weighing explanatory power against ontological economy.

limits: The problem of universals remains unresolved, with each position paying a price and facing objections. Platonic realism must account for the nature of a transcendent realm and the relation of instantiation by which particulars participate in Forms, and it faces regress worries, notably the Third Man argument, which threatens an infinite regress of Forms. Aristotelian realism must explain how a single universal can be wholly present in many places at once. Nominalism must explain objective resemblance and predication without universals, and its varieties face their own difficulties: resemblance nominalism confronts the companionship and imperfect-community problems raised by Nelson Goodman, and austere nominalism is charged with simply refusing to answer the question. Trope theory must explain resemblance among tropes without reintroducing a universal. Some attributions and terms reward care: ostrich is a pejorative label for austere nominalism, the Third Man appears in Plato's Parmenides and is sharpened in Aristotle, and Bradley's regress is a further worry best attributed with care. So the problem of universals robustly asks whether repeatable universals exist, understood as an ancient and open problem where realism, nominalism, and trope theory each face serious objections.
misreadings: The problem of universals is not merely a verbal dispute about words; it asks whether there really exist repeatable entities that many things share, a substantive ontological question. Realism is not committed to a Platonic separate realm, since Aristotelian realism locates universals in their instances. And nominalism is not the denial that things resemble one another, only the denial that a shared universal explains the resemblance, so treating the problem as verbal, realism as necessarily Platonic, or nominalism as denying resemblance, misreads it.
origin: The ancient metaphysical problem, the one over many from Plato, of whether the shared features of many particulars are grounded in repeatable universals or explained by particulars alone, dividing realism, nominalism, and trope theory.
